headline: Canarsie Pier by Kayak: Snapper Blues Everywhere, Bass Still Playing Hard to Get
subhead: I fished three access points this week and the story was the same everywhere — the bay's alive with bait, but the resident bass haven't caught up yet.
body_markdown:
I put the kayak in at Canarsie Pier Tuesday morning, before the heat got stupid, because that's the one launch in this whole bay where I can paddle out, drift the flats, and be back at the truck before the sun turns the parking lot into a griddle. It's also the best seat in the house for watching what the bait's doing, and this week the bait's doing plenty — peanut bunker pushed thick against the pier pilings, snapper blues slashing through them from first light till the boat traffic picks up around eight.

We called this one last week — said the snappers were thick in the shallows and it was a sign the bigger bluefish push filtering through the Sound would eventually show up here too. Well, the snappers are still thick, maybe thicker. Little guys, four to seven inches, absolutely relentless on anything shiny. If you've got a kid who needs a fishing win, tie on a 1/8-ounce Kastmaster or a sliver of Gulp on a snapper rig and work the edges of the pier pilings on the last two hours of the incoming. You will not get skunked. What we haven't seen yet is those snappers translating into a real run of cocktail blues inside the bay itself — that piece is still a maybe, not a yes.

The bass story is more complicated, and I want to be straight with you about it instead of blowing smoke. We flagged back on the 7th that the resident stripers had mostly cleared out of the bay for cooler water elsewhere in the Bight, and that's held up. If you're paddling or wading the flats off Canarsie or up around the Cross Bay Bridge marsh edges expecting bass, you're going to be disappointed most days right now. Water's warm, bay's shallow, and bass don't love that combination in mid-August no matter how much bait is stacked up.

Where it's different is at the current-driven structure, and that's exactly what we said would happen once the tide built strength into the new moon on the 12th. I fished the outgoing at Marine Parkway Bridge Thursday evening and there's a real bite happening in that rip line under the span — schooner bass, mostly 20 to 26 inches, holding tight to the shadow lines on the pilings and picking off peanut bunker as the current rips them through. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, white or bunker-pattern — cast up-current and swung through the seam, is the move. So is a soft plastic, something like a 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a light jig head, worked slow just off bottom in that 12 to 18 feet of water right off the fenders. Best window is the first two hours of the outgoing, right as the sun's dropping — that's when the bait gets pinched through the narrows and the bass stack up to ambush it. It's not a blitz. It's a real, workable bite if you're there at the right two hours and willing to grind a little.

Rockaway Beach has been more about bluefish and bunker pods running the wash than any real bass presence yet. I walked a stretch near the 90s Thursday morning and watched bunker schools nervous-water their way down the beach with birds working overhead — no visible blitz, but enough activity that I'd keep an eye on that corridor. If a real bass push does show up ahead of the fall run, that's usually where it announces itself first, with gulls diving on peanut bunker getting pushed against the sand.

Fluke fishing in the bay is holding at modest-but-honest. I worked the channel edge outside Rockaway Inlet on the last of an outgoing tide with a bucktail-and-Gulp combo — white bucktail, chartreuse Gulp trailer, dragged slow along the 15 to 22 foot channel drop — and picked at fish, nothing over three pounds but enough keepers mixed with shorts to call it a real pattern. If you're boat fishing, work the deeper cuts on the bay side of the inlet on the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still moving bait but not screaming.

Porgies have been steady but unspectacular around the mussel beds off Ruffle Bar and the flats east of the Cross Bay Bridge — small stuff on bloodworms and clam, good for a chowder pot, not much else to report there. Blackfish are still weeks off; that bite doesn't turn on here till the water cools into fall. Weakfish have been incidental at best — a couple caught mixed in with the fluke bite near the inlet channel, nothing to plan a trip around.

Looking ahead, I don't expect the bay's resident bass situation to change much until water temps start easing, which realistically means early-to-mid September around here. What I do expect to sharpen is that Marine Parkway Bridge bite, because the tidal flow is still building off this new moon and that rip under the span only gets better with more current behind it. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd be on the bridge at the top of the outgoing with metal in hand. For everyone else, the kayak-and-snapper program at Canarsie is about as sure a thing as this bay offers right now — just don't expect those little blues to turn into anything bigger just yet.
